Question: Which stadium in India was developed for very unique reasons?
Answer: Brabourne Stadium and Wankhede Stadium….two Cricket Stadiums next to each other in Marine Drive, Mumbai!! How could that happen? Answer: “EGO” A short story on Brabourne Stadium and Wankhede Stadium. Brabourne Stadium was built in the 1930's and was part of the prestigious Cricket Club of India. (CCI) It was the Lords of India. A fine stadium planned and executed brilliantly. After Independence, Test matches involving India were played at Brabourne Stadium. Bombay Cricket Association (BCA) and CCI had a deal regarding allocation of seats and revenues from the stadium. It was all going fine but in the late 1960's, BCA asked CCI for more ticket's allotment. CCI refused. But CCI refused, stating that they spend a significant amount on ground maintenance and any concession would cause the club to lose revenue. The BCA was so annoyed with this unreasonable behavior. However, in 1973–74, things got pretty intense when CCI President Vijay Merchant, the former Indian cricketer, refused SK Wankhede’s proposal to host charity matches for MLAs at the Brabourne Stadium. A heated argument followed, and Wankhede said, “If you continue this unfair treatment, then we will build our own stadium.” Then Merchant said, “You Marathi people won’t be able to do it. You don’t understand anything about cricket.” This insulting reply hurt Wankhede the most. He then convinced the general body of BCA to construct its own stadium in Mumbai. It made no economic sense, and Wankhede wanted a new stadium. It was considered impossible. But he wanted to do it. He secured permission to construct a stadium next to Brabourne Stadium. He even managed Cement: A commodity in so much scarcity that builders often fantasized about it. Even funds were arranged. No evidence is there on source of funds, but it is said that the funds came from the "number 2" accounts (black money) from various patrons of the party. Construction happened very fast. And in 1974-75, it opened for international cricket. A stadium built due to Ego!! Ref: Hindustan Times Article: How a dispute led to the creation of Wankhede Stadium - HT School

Question: What is the most important factor that shaped Putin into the leader he is today?
Answer: It is Putin’s childhood that shaped him into the dangerous leader he is today. Putin was born on October 7, 1952. He was born in Leningrad (now St Petersburg). Putin grew up in poverty, and the dilapidated Soviet block of flats he lived in was infested with rats. In Putin’s 2000 book First Person: An Astonishingly Frank Self-Portrait, he writes: Once I spotted a huge rat and pursued it down the hall until I drove it into a corner. It had nowhere to run. Suddenly it lashed around and threw itself at me. I was surprised and frightened. Now the rat was chasing me. Luckily, I was a little faster and I managed to slam the door shut in its nose. There, on that stair landing, I got a quick and lasting lesson in the meaning of the word “cornered.” Vladimir and Lyudmila Putin in their youth He learnt his fighting lessons in the early years of his life. Vladimir was small for his age and therefore, unsurprisingly, was bullied. He would regularly get into brawls with neighbor kids. He learned lessons that he has followed ever since – “to take on any and all adversaries, never to retreat, and to fight to the finish.” In school days, Putin once hung on the balcony of the fifth floor of the school building for a bet. He fought better than anyone, and once he stood up for the girls and fought with a gym teacher. Putin was bullied until he started studying martial arts. He got a black belt in Judo and his group was nicknamed as a ‘Jodocracy’. His best friend from school: He could get into a fight with anyone… He had no fear… If some hulking guy offended him, he would jump straight at him – scratch him, bite him, pull out clumps of his hair. Putin reportedly loved reading about spies, and wanted to become one before he was even out of school. At 16, he volunteered for the KGB and after studying law and economics, he ended up working for them as a spy. A fellow KGB officer Pavel Koshelev, said: His most outstanding trait, I would say, was his fighting spirit and his strong will to achieve his goals. Vladimir Putin’s Family Life: I Putin was a ‘miracle boy.’ Putin’s mother Maria gave birth to him in a hospital where 1 in 50 newborns died. Maria had already lost two baby sons and was overjoyed when Putin arrived. Maria almost died of starvation once as Putin’s father was away fighting. Putin was the apple of his parents’ eye. They didn’t have much, but whatever they had was given to Putin as a priority. They shared their home with two other families, and his former school teacher said: There was no hot water, no bathtub. The toilet was horrendous. And it was so cold, awful. Putin with his parents. I Putin’s marriage life: Putin is ‘scrappy, very ambitious, very, very greedy’. Vladimir Putin married Lyudmila Putina, a former air hostess, in the mid-1980s and the pair had two daughters together. His split with his wife due to his ambition and work. He was married for 30 years. It seems fair to say that Putin puts nothing ahead of his own ambition and Russia’s success as a country. In the current climate – he said: “West’s support of Ukraine is the same as declaring war on Russia and it is very unsettling.” Vladimir Putin in 2016: 50 years ago the Leningrad street taught me a rule: if a fight is inevitable you have to throw the first punch.”
